content:
Cambridge Analytica is the scandal. What sits underneath it is the revelation, and I think the revelation is considerably larger than the scandal that exposed it.

The scandal is straightforward. A political consultancy harvested data from millions of Facebook users without meaningful consent and used it to target political messaging during elections. This is bad, people are right to be angry, and there will be hearings and fines and tightened regulations. I expect all of that, and I expect it to change almost nothing.

The revelation is that public cognition now runs on private infrastructure. The way a country encounters information, forms opinions, argues with itself and decides its own future happens inside systems that are privately owned, algorithmically managed, and unreachable by any democratic process at all. We've handed over the machinery a society uses to think, and we did it without a single vote being taken on the question.

I want to be careful about how this happened, because the popular account is wrong in a way that leads to bad remedies. There was no conspiracy. Nobody elected these companies to organise public discourse, and nobody had to - they became the infrastructure of public life through convenience, network effects, and the plain fact that they are extremely good products that billions of people wanted to use. Several billion individually reasonable choices produced a collective transfer that nobody chose. That's a much harder problem than malice, because there's no one to remove.

**The Optimisation Problem**

The same care applies to the algorithm. It doesn't want anyone angry. It doesn't want anything. It promotes content that generates engagement, engagement correlates with emotional arousal, and emotional arousal correlates with precisely the mental states least suited to democratic deliberation. What we're watching is an optimisation function producing a side effect at civilisational scale, which is a genuinely novel kind of problem and one our institutions have no experience with.

This is also why Cambridge Analytica shouldn't be understood as an aberration - a bad actor exploiting a system that would otherwise have been fine. Build infrastructure that can model human psychology at scale, make it available to anyone with a budget, and someone will eventually use it to move an election. That was always going to happen. What surprises me is that anyone was surprised.

The standard remedy on offer is content moderation at scale: more reviewers, better policies, clearer rules. I understand the appeal and I don't think it touches the actual problem. Under that remedy a handful of private entities still decide what several billion people see, and the only change is that they now do it more carefully. That gives us the same concentration with better manners, which isn't accountability by any definition I recognise.

Nobody knows for certain what a decade of this does to a democracy. The honest researchers disagree with each other, the effect sizes are contested, and anyone claiming confidence in either direction is overselling. But when the uncertainty is this wide and the thing at stake is a society's capacity to reason with itself, cautious action is more sensible than waiting for proof that will arrive too late to act on.

**A Portability Regime**

The specific measure I'd argue for is narrower than most of what's being proposed, and I think it would accomplish considerably more.

The single greatest source of platform power has very little to do with the algorithm or the data. Leaving costs you everyone you know, and almost nobody will pay that. A user who dislikes what a platform has become faces a choice between the product and their entire social world, and almost nobody chooses the second. Every other problem - the engagement optimisation, the opaque ranking, the indifference to complaints - persists downstream of that one fact. A company whose users genuinely cannot leave has no structural reason to serve them well, however decent the people inside it happen to be.

So: once a service passes a threshold of national significance, it should be required to make identity, social graph and content portable on published technical terms, and to interoperate with competitors who meet the same standard. A person should be able to move platforms the way they move between phone carriers - keeping their number, keeping their contacts, losing nothing but the interface.

We've done this before, which is why I think it's realistic rather than utopian. Number portability was fiercely resisted by telecommunications incumbents on grounds of technical impossibility and security risk, and once it existed the market it created was better for everyone including, eventually, the incumbents. Nobody today finds it remarkable that you can ring someone on a different network.

The mechanism matters more than the sentiment. Portability doesn't require a regulator to decide what speech is acceptable, which is a job no democratic government should want and none has done well. It doesn't require anyone to audit an algorithm they lack the expertise to understand. It changes the incentive directly: a platform whose users can leave without cost has to earn them every day, and platforms that have to earn users behave differently from platforms that own them. Alongside it I'd let people choose or supply their own ranking, so that one company's optimisation target stops being an entire country's information diet by default.

**The Railroad Precedent**

In the nineteenth century the railroads transformed the physical infrastructure of civilisation. They connected markets, moved goods, built cities, and concentrated enormous power in the companies that owned the rails. The barons became, for a period, more powerful than the governments nominally regulating them - setting prices, determining routes, deciding which towns would prosper and which would empty out.

The democratic response took decades to arrive: antitrust law, the Interstate Commerce Commission, and the eventual recognition that infrastructure this important couldn't be left wholly to private control. We are in the railroad baron phase of digital infrastructure, and the regulators are as outmatched now as they were then.

What I take from that history is that it was solved, by ordinary democratic means, within the lifetime of the people who first complained about it. That's not a small thing to know.

From Australia the picture has a sharper edge, because we aren't merely failing to regulate the platforms - we have no domestic platforms to regulate. The servers are in Virginia and Oregon, the algorithms are written in California, and the decisions determining what Australians read are made in rooms where no Australian sits. This didn't happen to us. We chose it the way we chose to let manufacturing go: by integrating enthusiastically into systems built elsewhere and treating digital infrastructure as a commercial product rather than a strategic asset.

The scandal will fade. The hearings will conclude, the fines will be paid, the news cycle will move on, and the underlying arrangement will remain exactly where it is. The question worth holding onto is whether self-governance is possible when the infrastructure of public thought sits beyond the reach of the public.

I don't think that question is settled, and I don't think it settles itself. We built the rules for the presses and the rails and the telephone networks, each time later than we should have and each time successfully. There's no reason this is the one we can't do - only a shrinking window in which to do it.
